title: Painting
strapline: Colour that swirls, drips and surprises — brave marks and proud painters.
intent: Discover colour change first-hand: what happens when the yellow touches the blue, and how to make that green again
Move from whole-arm easel sweeps to controlled fine brushwork, at each child's own pace
Learn that painted marks can carry meaning — a name, a story, a portrait of mummy
Make real creative choices: which colour, which tool, which paper — and own the result
Enjoy paint as a sensory material in its own right, especially for our youngest painters
Talk about paintings — their own and other people's — noticing colour, detail and feeling
implementation: Offer primary colours plus white and let children mix their own palettes, rather than always pre-mixing for them
Keep both on offer: easels for big-arm work and table-top fine brushes for detail — children need the shoulder before the fingers
Say "tell me about your painting", never "what is it?" — and scribe the child's words on the back
Name techniques as children use them: dab, sweep, drip, blend, swirl
Vary the tools and the canvas — rollers, sponges, feathers, toothbrushes; huge paper, tiny paper, paper on the floor and the fence
Value process over product: not every painting needs to go home flat, finished and recognisable
Set up self-portrait provision with mirrors and a proper skin-tone palette every child can find themselves in
key_questions: What do you think will happen if the yellow touches the blue?
How did you make that green? Could you make it again?
Which brush will make the thinnest line?
Tell me about this part here — what's happening?
What colours will you mix for your own skin and hair?

impact.text: Our youngest painters explore paint on their own terms — spreading, layering, painting their hands as happily as the paper — with whole-arm, fist-grip movements.
Children paint freely and give the marks meaning afterwards: "it's a storm", "that's daddy's car".
Painting becomes intentional — "I'm painting mummy" — announced before the brush touches the paper.
Children choose their own colours, tools and paper, and mix colours deliberately to see what happens.
Children notice and describe change as colours blend — "it went brown!" — picking up words like swirl, blend and fade along the way.
Brush control grows: a comfortable, effective grip, thin lines when they're wanted, and paint that (mostly) stays where it was aimed.
Children talk about their own paintings in detail and stop to notice what a friend has done: "how did you do that bit?"
Older painters decide what to paint, how, and when it's finished — and their marks carry meaning they can read back to you.

enhancements: Just two primary colours plus white at the easel for a week — watch the mixing theories emerge
Water and chunky decorating brushes on the fence and slabs for zero-cost giant painting
Mirrors and skin-tone paints for self-portraits, displayed at child height in real frames
Ice-cube paints in summer — colour, melting and mixing in one go
Conkers or marbles rolled through paint in a tray for trajectory painters
A pale wash over yesterday's dried painting to discover layering
An artist's postcard beside the easel — not to copy, but to talk about: "what do you notice?"

playing_exploring: Paint invites full-sensory investigation — colour, texture, drip and smell — with no right answer waiting
Children experiment with tools and surfaces nobody told them to combine
active_learning: Children chase an effect — the exact green, the thinnest line — and keep adjusting until they get it
creating_thinking: Colour mixing is theory-testing: children predict, try, observe and revise
Children develop their own visual ideas and return to favourite subjects, refining them over weeks
